author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1: Structural Anatomy of the Heart
modules.description: An exploration of the structural anatomy of the human heart, focusing on chambers, valves, and major vessels.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart.
Students will identify the four heart valves.
Students will identify the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
instructions: Use the Next button to advance through the structural overview of chambers, valves, and vessels.

clips.changeMeaning: Initialize the scene and introduce the heart structure
clips.narration: Welcome to the Human Heart anatomy lab. In front of you is a 3D model of the human heart, continuously rotating. Notice its overall shape, orientation, and the major vessels emerging from its superior surface.

components.text: The Four Chambers: Right & Left Atria and Ventricles

clips.changeMeaning: Update label to focus on the four chambers
clips.narration: The heart is divided into four main chambers. The two superior receiving chambers are the right and left atria. The two inferior pumping chambers are the right and left ventricles.

components.text: The Four Valves: Tricuspid, Pulmonary, Mitral, Aortic

clips.changeMeaning: Update label to focus on the four valves
clips.narration: Separating these chambers and vessels are four crucial valves that ensure one-way blood flow. The atrioventricular valves are the tricuspid and mitral valves, while the semilunar valves are the pulmonary and aortic valves.

components.text: Major Vessels: Vena Cava, Pulmonary Trunk/Veins, Aorta

clips.changeMeaning: Update label to focus on the major vessels
clips.narration: Finally, major vessels transport blood to and from the heart. Observe the superior and inferior vena cava, the pulmonary arteries and veins, and the massive aorta arching over the top.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2: Path of Blood Through the Heart
modules.description: Trace the path that blood takes through the heart's dual circulation system.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit.
instructions: Follow the path of the blood indicator (sphere).
Notice the color change from blue (deoxygenated) to red (oxygenated) as blood returns from the lungs.

components.text: 1. Deoxygenated Blood enters Right Atrium via Vena Cava

clips.changeMeaning: Show deoxygenated blood entering the right atrium from the vena cava
clips.narration: Let's trace the dual-loop circulation. First, deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circuit enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior vena cava. Watch the blue indicator representing this deoxygenated blood.

components.text: 2. Tricuspid Valve -> Right Ventricle -> Pulmonary Valve -> Lungs

clips.changeMeaning: Move blood indicator to the right ventricle, then simulate pumping to lungs
clips.narration: Blood flows through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The right ventricle then pumps it through the pulmonary semilunar valve into the pulmonary arteries, directing it to the lungs for oxygenation.

components.text: 3. Oxygenated Blood returns to Left Atrium via Pulmonary Veins

clips.changeMeaning: Change blood indicator to red (oxygenated) and move to left atrium
clips.narration: In the lungs, blood picks up oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. This newly oxygenated blood, now shown in red, returns via the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.

components.text: 4. Mitral Valve -> Left Ventricle -> Aortic Valve -> Body

clips.changeMeaning: Move blood indicator to left ventricle and out the aorta
clips.narration: From the left atrium, blood passes through the mitral, or bicuspid, valve into the left ventricle. Finally, the left ventricle forcefully pumps the blood through the aortic valve and into the aorta, distributing it to the entire body.

modules.description: Examine the relationship between form and function by comparing ventricular myocardium thickness and observing valve action.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Students will explain why the left ventricle has a thicker myocardium than the right ventricle.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow.
instructions: Compare the left and right ventricular walls on the cross-section.

components.text: Form and Function: Myocardium and Valves
Notice the Left Ventricle's thicker myocardium

clips.changeMeaning: Highlight the difference in ventricular wall thickness
clips.narration: Let's look at the heart's muscular wall, the myocardium. Notice how the wall of the left ventricle is substantially thicker than that of the right ventricle. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs, while the left ventricle must generate enough pressure to perfuse the entire systemic circuit.

components.text: Valves snap shut to prevent backflow during the cardiac cycle

clips.changeMeaning: Switch view to the valves to discuss backflow prevention
clips.narration: As these thick muscles contract, the valves play a critical role. When the ventricles contract, the atrioventricular valves snap shut to prevent blood from flowing backward into the atria. Conversely, when the ventricles relax, the semilunar valves close to prevent blood in the aorta and pulmonary arteries from falling back into the heart.
